name: Rafael Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season, but now it's tupping, so the rams are in with the ewes and I'm checking them every morning. I'm out at first light on the quad bike with the two dogs, Bess and Moss, going round the in-bye fields, which are the walled ones near the farmhouse. A couple of days a week we gather off the fell, the open hill, which takes four of us and the dogs most of a day. I like the hill, I like that nobody's watching you. What wears me out is the weather, it's either sideways rain or fog so thick you can't see your own dog.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and about you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Highfell, about 900 hectares of hill and common grazing with eleven hundred ewes, owned by Tom Brennan, who's seventy. I've been there four years and I'm the junior, so Ellis, the head shepherd, gets the hard calls and I get told off. I live with my girlfriend Kerry, she works on the front desk at the vet's in town. We've got a little stone cottage that's paid for, because my grandad sold some land and left me a share.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, or computers much, for the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've never asked a computer anything in my life. We've got an electronic reader for the ear tags and I'll be honest, I still write the numbers in a notebook as well, because the reader's dropped them twice. Kerry does the online banking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd have bet on anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go. You can't gather a fell with a chatbot. I'd say it in the pub and leave it there, I'm not one for online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the stuff that worries me isn't computers. It's the lamb price, and whether the government keeps paying hill farms to look after the land, because without that money nobody up here makes a living. And wool's worth next to nothing now, we pay more to shear them than we get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd also like to buy fifty ewes of my own next autumn and run them on a bit of rented ground near the village, which would be about six thousand with the rent. That's how you start, Tom says, a few of your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the job you're still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lambing on the hill when the snow comes late. Ellis can tell which ewe's going to have trouble just from how she's standing. I've been watching ewes stand for four years and they all look the same to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tag reader dropped the numbers. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice it just lost a whole morning's work, two hundred tags. Tom shouted, and it wasn't the machine he shouted at. So now I write them down too, and I'm not changing that.

S0.say: I'd say you can't gather a fell with a chatbot. I'd say it in the pub and leave it there, since I'm not one for posting online.
S0.think: I think the real worries are the lamb price and whether the government keeps paying hill farms to look after the land. Wool is worth next to nothing, and computers aren't the problem.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is. Plans to buy fifty ewes of his own next autumn and run them on rented ground near the village, at about six thousand including rent.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing changed from yesterday.
S0.quote: I've been watching ewes stand for four years and they all look the same to me.
S0.fieldNote: He was unbothered and quick to name the things he actually worries about: lamb prices, hill payments and worthless wool. The story of the tag reader losing a morning's work explains his distrust of technology better than any opinion. His plan to buy a few ewes of his own shows quiet ambition beneath the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mm. That's more the lowland farms, I'd have thought. Not so much us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone gets excited. Every few years there's a new gadget that's going to change everything, and half of them end up in the back of the shed. I'd say that to Ellis and he'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the hill's slower to change than anywhere, so I think we'd mostly carry on. But the farm two valleys over tried a drone to gather sheep last year. It scattered the whole flock into the bracken, but it'll get better, and that does bother me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, but I'd put more aside, maybe two hundred extra a month, in case. I wouldn't learn anything new until I saw it work on a farm like ours, with my own eyes. If Tom bought something, I'd learn it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. A small thing in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Tom asked you to learn to fly a drone for gathering, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, because he's the boss. But I'd take the dogs along. If the drone scatters them into the bracken again, Bess can fetch them back and the drone can watch her do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many on the hill, to be honest. Maybe the people in the auction mart office, if the selling all goes online. I don't know enough about it to say.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone gets excited. Every few years there's a gadget that will change everything, and half end up in the back of the shed.
S1.think: I think the hill changes slower than anywhere, so we'd mostly carry on. But a nearby farm tried a drone for gathering sheep, and even though it failed, it will improve, and that bothers me a bit.
S1.do: Keeps working and saves about two hundred extra a month just in case. Waits to see any new tool working on a similar farm before learning it, unless his boss buys one.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy, with a small worry at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: If the drone scatters them into the bracken again, Bess can fetch them back and the drone can watch her do it.
S1.fieldNote: His reflex is to wait for proof on a farm like his own, and the failed drone gather is the story he tells himself. He'd learn a new tool only if his boss bought it, and even then he'd bring the dogs. He admitted plainly that he doesn't know enough about the auction side to judge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even for the hill? With robots walking up there?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not lose our heads. People said tractors would empty the countryside and there were still people. I'd say it calmly, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if a robot can gather the fell in fog, Tom sells the flock to some company and retires, and that's me done. Ellis would maybe get kept on to watch the machines. I'm the junior, so I'm the one that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shelve the fifty ewes and keep the money in the bank. I'd cut back, no new quad, no holiday, and Kerry and I would live on her wage if we had to, with the cottage paid for. After it arrived, I'd go and help my dad on his bit of land and wait to see what's left, because I've no idea what I'd retrain as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than I'd let on in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, because I'm slow with new things, I know that. I've never typed a question into a computer. Two years isn't long enough for me to start and catch up. Somebody quicker might manage. Not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Bess and Moss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They stay with me, whatever happens. I'd keep them if I had to live on beans. A dog that's worked the hill isn't a pet, she's a colleague, and you don't sell a colleague.

S2.say: I'd say let's not lose our heads, because people said tractors would empty the countryside and there were still people. I'd say it calmly, since someone has to.
S2.think: I think if a robot can gather the fell in fog, my boss sells the flock and retires, and as the junior I'm the one who goes. The head shepherd might be kept on to watch the machines.
S2.do: Shelves plans to buy his own ewes and keeps savings in the bank. Cuts spending and lives on his partner's wage if needed, then helps on his father's land and waits to see what's left.
S2.feel: Anxious, more than he'd show in public.
S2.quote: I've never typed a question into a computer. Two years isn't long enough for me to start and catch up.
S2.fieldNote: His public line is calm and steadying, but privately he expects to be the first to go. He was frank that he's too slow with technology to retrain in two years, and he didn't dress that up. The paid-off cottage and his partner's wage are what keep him from alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's be sensible about it. Don't throw money at every new thing, but don't pretend it's not coming. I'd say that to Tom, and to Kerry's dad, who thinks I'm soft for even worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the old crafts might last longest, the stuff that's slow and fiddly and in awkward places. Dry stone walling, hedge laying. People with big houses pay good money for a proper wall, and there's miles of them up here falling down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask old Jim Pearson, who's done walls up here for forty years, if I could work with him on Saturdays and learn properly. I'd still buy the fifty ewes, because a few years of my own flock is still worth having. And I'd keep putting the extra two hundred away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with my hands, so less than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn walling properly, which takes about three years to be any good. Jim says a wall's only as good as the stones you didn't use. I'd like five years to understand what he means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: But in this picture robots reach hands-on work too. Couldn't they build walls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, by the end. I don't know, I'm being honest. But I'd rather be holding a stone than sitting at home waiting to find out.

S3.say: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's be sensible: don't throw money at every new thing, but don't pretend it isn't coming. I'd say that to my boss and my partner's father.
S3.think: I think old crafts in awkward places might last longest, like dry stone walling and hedge laying. People with big houses pay well for a proper wall, and there are miles of them falling down.
S3.do: Asks a veteran local waller to teach him on Saturdays over the next few years. Still buys fifty ewes of his own and keeps saving an extra two hundred a month.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less so, because he'd have something to do with his hands.
S3.quote: Jim says a wall's only as good as the stones you didn't use. I'd like five years to understand what he means.
S3.fieldNote: Five years let him pick something that suits him: a slow, physical craft he can learn from an older man. When pressed that robots could build walls too, he admitted he didn't know and chose action over waiting. His centre outlook shows in his advice to be neither hasty nor in denial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Tom won't be farming then, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so there's no excuse for anyone panicking or for the government doing nothing. Plan it, keep it steady. That's all I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think land's the thing. My grandad always said they're not making any more of it. If I had ten years, I'd want to own a small hill farm of my own, even if the work changes, because whoever owns the ground has a say in what happens on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving hard for five or six years and then try to buy a small farm, maybe forty hectares with a house, using the cottage as security. I'd keep the walling going on the side and keep my own flock growing. And I'd keep an eye on what the robots actually do on the hill before I spent anything on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Ten years is something a person can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm not just a worker that gets let go. With ten years I can stop being the shepherd and start being the owner, even if it's a small bit of rough ground. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you've never used a computer for work. If you owned a farm in 2036, would that hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Kerry would do the computer side, or I'd learn slowly. Don't tell Ellis I said that.

S4.say: I'd say there's time, so there's no excuse for panic or for the government doing nothing. Plan it and keep it steady, and that's all I'd ask.
S4.think: I think land is the thing to hold, as my grandfather said. With ten years I'd want to own a small hill farm, because whoever owns the ground has a say in what happens on it.
S4.do: Saves hard for five or six years and then tries to buy a small farm of about forty hectares, using the cottage as security. Keeps walling on the side, grows his own flock and waits to see robots work on the hill before buying any.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, with a timeframe he feels he can work with.
S4.quote: With ten years I can stop being the shepherd and start being the owner, even if it's a small bit of rough ground.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns him from a worker who expects to be let go into someone planning to own land. The idea comes from his grandfather and fits his cautious, practical nature. He conceded, half joking, that he'd probably learn the computer side in the end, but wanted that kept from his boss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm slow with new things and two years is no time at all. What would help is the government keeping hill farm payments tied to people looking after the land, not just to how much the land produces, and someone giving us a straight answer early, not after it's happened.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hill itself. Who keeps the walls up and the drains clear if there's no one living up there? A robot might gather the sheep, but I've never seen anyone pay a robot to care about a place.

headlineQuote: If the drone scatters them into the bracken again, Bess can fetch them back and the drone can watch her do it.
portrait: Rafael Quinn is a 27-year-old junior shepherd on a hill farm with eleven hundred ewes, who works the fell with his two dogs and has never asked a computer anything. He owns a small cottage outright with his partner Kerry, thanks to his grandfather's land sale, and he's pragmatic and slow to blame anyone. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption he mostly carries on, saving a little more and waiting to see machines prove themselves on a farm like his. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, because he knows he can't learn new things that fast, so he cuts back and leans on family. With five years he'd learn dry stone walling, and with ten he'd save to buy a small hill farm of his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he is slow with new things and two years would leave him no time to learn anything else.
whatWouldHelp: Hill farm payments tied to people caring for the land rather than to output, and a straight answer from government early on.
